methodological_rigor.justification: The prospective multicenter cohort design (MoST program, n=3383) is appropriate for the question, with pre-specified STROBE adherence, trial registration (ACTRN12616000908437), and a reasonable stratification into cohort A (no further therapy) and cohort B (received therapy) to avoid immortal-time comparisons. Statistical handling is competent: time-dependent multivariable Cox models adjust for age, ECOG, cancer type, prior lines, and prior matched therapy, with Kaplan-Meier and log-rank for unadjusted comparisons, plus sensitivity analyses (patients dying pre-results, same-therapy restriction, updated TOPOGRAPH tiering). Key limitations: no a priori power calculation is reported, there is no explicit multiplicity correction across the many tier-level subgroup comparisons (tiers 1-2, 3, 3B, 4, R2), and residual confounding by indication is inherent to observational matched vs unmatched comparisons despite the time-dependent covariate. Methods for handling missing covariate data are not described, and the comparator (unmatched) heterogeneity is only partially addressed.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual prospective cohort study drawn from a national precision oncology program, placing it at Oxford LoE 2b. The clinical relevance is high: it addresses a pressing practical question — how to prioritize genomically matched therapies by evidence tier — using the patient-relevant endpoint of overall survival in a heavily pretreated, predominantly rare-cancer population (71.7%). The finding that OS benefit is confined to tier 1-3A matches and absent for off-label repurposing (tier 3B) directly informs molecular tumor board practice and corroborates ESMO/ESCAT-aligned guidelines. The translational impact is immediate for structured decision-making, though confirmation in randomized settings (e.g., ROME, NCI-MATCH follow-ups) is still needed.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is appropriate for this observational cohort and is explicitly cited; the manuscript provides eligibility criteria, participant flow (Figure 1), prespecified subgroups, censoring rules, and sensitivity analyses, with trial registration and ethics approval reported. Minor gaps include no explicit sample-size justification, limited description of missing-data handling, and incomplete reporting of how tiering versioning affected individual patients. Data and code availability are not described in the retained manuscript text — the TOPOGRAPH version is specified (AU 20220828) but patient-level data, analytic R code, and supplementary materials beyond eFigures are not pointed to a repository in the blinded body, limiting the reproducibility posture.

novelty_literature.justification: The study makes a meaningful but incremental contribution to a crowded precision-oncology registry/matching literature (SHIVA, MOSCATO, MyPathway, I-PREDICT, Know Your Tumor, WINTHER, TAPUR, NCI-MATCH, ProfiLER, ROME are all cited). The specific novelty lies in operationalizing the TOPOGRAPH tiering framework at scale (n=3383), demonstrating that OS benefit is restricted to tier 1-3A matches while tier 3B off-label repurposing confers no benefit (and possibly harm, aHR 1.40), with enrichment for rare cancers. This is a useful empirical refinement and population extension rather than a new mechanism or framework — ESCAT already provides a comparable tiering system (cited as reference 34), which the authors themselves identify as a limitation.

writing_presentation.justification: The main body is organized logically with clear methods, results aligned with prespecified subgroups, and informative figure captions. However, the abstract is poorly structured for a blinded manuscript — it contains apparent duplication/repetition (the research question, population, results, and conclusion appear in overlapping blocks typical of a JAMA-style abstract rendered incorrectly). There is also a redaction/text error in the results section ("2065 patients (61.0%) who [REDACTED] patients (39.0%)") that disrupts interpretation of cohort flow. Some headings are awkward (e.g., "Survival Association Between Harborage of Actionable Biomarkers"), and discussion sentences occasionally overreach for an observational finding.

key_strengths: Large (n=3383), prospective, nationally recruited cohort enriched for rare/refractory cancers (71.7%)
Appropriate time-dependent Cox modeling to mitigate immortal-time bias with multivariable adjustment
Clinically actionable finding: OS benefit confined to tier 1-3A matches; tier 3B off-label repurposing not beneficial (aHR 1.40, P=.047)
Prespecified subgroups and multiple sensitivity analyses (pre-results deaths, same-therapy restriction, updated tiering)
key_concerns: No a priori power calculation and no explicit multiplicity correction across many tier-level comparisons
Residual confounding by indication inherent to observational matched vs unmatched comparisons; missing-data handling not described
Data/code availability not clearly stated in retained text, limiting reproducibility
Novelty is incremental relative to prior registry/matching studies (SHIVA, MOSCATO, MyPathway, I-PREDICT, ROME, ESCAT)
Abstract shows structural duplication and a redaction artifact in cohort flow narrative
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, clinically relevant observational study with a practice-informing message justifies a tier 2 ceiling (e.g., venues around JCO Precision Oncology / ESMO Open / Nature Communications), but incremental novelty relative to the dense precision-oncology registry literature, absence of randomization, and reproducibility gaps prevent a tier 1 placement. Minor revisions to address multiplicity, missing-data handling, and data/code availability would strengthen the submission.
